869.title: Alphonsus Liguori (1696–1787)
869.hook: a lawyer turned priest who taught moral theology with mercy
869.howItsDone: Redemptorist priests and brothers still preach parish missions and hear confessions, and Catholic seminarians and confessors often study Alphonsus's moral theology; his short prayer books, like his visits to the Blessed Sacrament, are still prayed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jansenism: a strict movement that made communion feel like a prize for the nearly perfect. Your line was not a reward. What did you accept today without earning it? Today, a man who fought that same strictness from inside the confessional. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

Lawyers are trained to read every line of a document. Tradition says one young lawyer in Naples, quick, well trained and from a noble family, missed one detail in a document and lost an important case because of it. Tradition says he walked out of court and stayed shut away for days, and that afterward he left the law for good. Not long after, he gave up his sword at a shrine of Our Lady and set out to become a priest. A lawyer who had just learned how it feels to be wrong in public. His name is Alphonsus Liguori.
screen: `A LAWYER IN NAPLES.` → `ONE OVERLOOKED DETAIL.` → `HE LEAVES THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Four turns in his story. First, the countryside. As a priest, Alphonsus went out to the poor villages and goatherds in the hills around Naples, people he felt the Church had left behind. To preach to them, he founded a congregation of priests and brothers named for the Most Holy Redeemer. Today they're called Redemptorists. Second, the confessional, and two ditches. Hearing confessions, he met two kinds of priest. Some were so strict that people left without absolution and stopped coming back. Others excused nearly everything. Neither one, he thought, actually helped a person get free. Third, the book. So the former lawyer did what lawyers do. He studied the cases. He wrote a long work of moral theology, weighing hard questions one by one, looking for the path between harshness and excuses. Where a law was truly in doubt, he argued, a person should not always be bound to the strictest answer. He taught that a confessor is a father and a physician as well as a judge. Fourth, mercy with a spine. Mercy for Alphonsus never meant pretending sin isn't real. It meant judging the way God judges. In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." And straight after: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged." The Church later named Alphonsus a Doctor of the Church. He also wrote simple books of prayer for ordinary people, and songs they could sing.
screen: `PREACHING TO THE FORGOTTEN POOR.` · `TOO HARSH, OR TOO LOOSE.` · `A LAWYER STUDIES THE CASES.` · `MERCY THAT STILL TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `BE YE THEREFORE MERCIFUL, AS YOUR FATHER ALSO IS MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: judge one person mercifully. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you judged recently, out loud or in your head. A coworker, a driver, a relative, a stranger online. Now do what Alphonsus did with his cases: become their lawyer for a minute. What don't you know about their day? What might they be carrying? You're not excusing anything. You're just letting the whole case into the room. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Alphonsus Liguori. A Naples lawyer turned priest, founder of the Redemptorists, who taught confessors to judge with mercy.
Your line: mercy in judging. Today, the next time a verdict forms in your head about someone, pause and ask for one more piece of the case before you close it. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

870.title: Louis de Montfort (1673–1716)
870.hook: to Jesus through Mary: a total consecration
870.howItsDone: Catholics who make Montfort's consecration usually follow a period of prayer and reading from his True Devotion to Mary, then consecrate themselves on a Marian feast, and some renew it each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alphonsus Liguori, the lawyer who studied hard cases so confessors would be kind. Your line was mercy in judging. Did you ask for one more piece of someone's case? Today, a wandering preacher with a rosary. Day eight hundred seventy.

Villagers are carrying earth in baskets up a hill in Brittany. A poor priest in a worn cassock has talked them into building a calvary: a mound, a path, a cross on top, so people can walk and pray the Passion. They dig, haul and build. Tradition says that on the eve of the blessing, an order arrives: tear it down. The authorities fear it could be used as a fort. Tradition says the priest took the news quietly and said, blessed be God. His name is Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort, and he is remembered for one phrase in particular.
screen: `VILLAGERS BUILD A CALVARY.` → `AN ORDER: TEAR IT DOWN.` → `BLESSED BE GOD.`

segments.voice: First, the preacher. Louis de Montfort spent his life on the road in western France, preaching missions in villages, teaching the rosary, writing hymns people could sing to tunes they already knew. Some bishops welcomed him. Others sent him away. He founded communities that carried on after him, among them the Daughters of Wisdom. Second, the phrase: to Jesus through Mary. In his book True Devotion to Mary, he is clear that the goal is Jesus. Mary is the way he chose, because, he wrote, she is the surest and gentlest road to her Son. Every true devotion to her, he says, ends in him. Third, the total gift. Montfort proposed a consecration: after a time of preparation, a person gives everything to Jesus through Mary's hands. Body, soul, possessions, even the good of one's prayers and good deeds, with nothing held back. Catholics still make this consecration, often on a feast of Mary. Pope John Paul II took his motto, Totus tuus, all yours, from this tradition. Fourth, what Mary herself says. In John's Gospel, at the wedding at Cana, she speaks to the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." She points away from herself. And at the cross, Jesus says to the beloved disciple, "Behold thy mother," and the disciple takes her as his own. Catholic tradition reads that as a gift to every disciple. Worship belongs to God alone, the Church teaches. Mary, in Montfort's picture, is the mother who walks you to her Son.
screen: `A PREACHER ON THE ROAD.` · `TO JESUS THROUGH MARY.` · `A TOTAL GIFT: TOTUS TUUS.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give Mary one day. Settle, and breathe. Walk through the rest of today in your mind, hour by hour: the work, the meals, the people, the dull stretches. If you pray, you can say the Hail Mary slowly, and as you do, hand each piece of the day to her, to carry to her Son. If you don't pray, choose one person who has mothered you, and offer the day in their honor, doing each task the way they'd hope to see it done. The bell holds the time.
Totus tuus. Latin for all yours, the total consecration to Jesus through Mary that Louis de Montfort taught, and the motto Pope John Paul II took from him.
Your line: to Jesus through Mary. Today, when a task feels small, do it the way Mary told the servants at Cana: whatever he tells you, do it. Day eight hundred seventy.

871.title: Junípero Serra, honestly
871.hook: founder of the California missions, canonized in 2015 amid pain for Indigenous communities
871.howItsDone: The Church keeps Saint Junípero Serra's memorial in its calendar, and in California some dioceses and parishes pair it with listening sessions, prayer and work alongside Native communities, whose members hold a range of views on his sainthood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Louis de Montfort, the wandering preacher who taught Totus tuus, all yours. Your line was to Jesus through Mary. Did you do a small task the way Mary told the servants at Cana? Today, a harder story, told honestly. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

A bronze friar lies on the grass of a California park. Protesters have pulled him off his base with ropes. In recent years, more than one statue of this man has come down. And yet the same man was declared a saint by Pope Francis, at a Mass in the United States. A saint to some Catholics. To some Native Californians, the face of what happened to their ancestors. Both are true at once, and today we don't get to pick one. The friar is Junípero Serra.
screen: `A STATUE PULLED DOWN.` → `A SAINT DECLARED.` → `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: First, the friar. Junípero Serra was a Franciscan from the island of Majorca. As a friar he took the name of Brother Juniper, a companion of Saint Francis. He was a teacher of theology who left it all to preach in New Spain. Tradition says he walked huge distances on an injured leg. He went north with Spanish soldiers and settlers and helped found a chain of missions along the California coast. Second, what Catholics honor. His zeal, his endurance, his poverty. When soldiers abused Native people near the missions, he traveled to Mexico City and asked the viceroy for rules to restrain them. At the canonization, Pope Francis praised him as a defender of the dignity of the native community. Third, what Native voices remember. The missions were part of Spain's colonial project. Baptized Native people were not free to leave. They were made to work, and could be whipped as punishment, something Serra himself defended in writing. Disease spread through the mission communities, and languages, ceremonies and ways of life were broken. For their descendants, this is not old history. It is family history. Pope Francis has also asked forgiveness for crimes committed against native peoples in the conquest of the Americas. Fourth, listening. The letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims, says: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." Telling Serra's story honestly means letting the people who carry the wound speak first. Some Catholics honor him. Some Native Catholics grieve his canonization. Both are inside the Church, and both deserve to be heard.
screen: `A FRIAR FROM MAJORCA.` · `WHAT CATHOLICS HONOR.` · `WHAT NATIVE FAMILIES REMEMBER.` · `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · then, large: `LET EVERY MAN BE SWIFT TO HEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen first. Settle, and breathe. Choose one Indigenous voice to listen to this week: a book, a recorded talk, a song, a local elder, a Native Catholic writing about the missions. Decide now which one, and when. Then rehearse the listening. Picture yourself hearing something that stings, and notice the reply that rises in you. Let it sit. Don't argue back, don't explain, just keep hearing. If you pray, you can hold Indigenous Catholics, and every family still carrying this history, before God. The bell holds the time.
Junípero Serra. The Franciscan who helped found the California missions, honored as a saint by the Church and remembered with pain by Native families.
Your line: listen first. Today, in one conversation where you disagree, let the other person finish completely before you answer. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

872.title: The Jesuits suppressed (1773)
872.hook: the pope dissolves the Jesuits under political pressure; they are restored in 1814
872.howItsDone: Jesuits today remember the suppression and restoration as part of their own story, and their schools, parishes and retreat houses often tell it to students and retreatants as a lesson in obedience and endurance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Junípero Serra, honestly: a saint to some, a wound to others, and both true. Your line was listen first. Did you let someone finish before you answered? Today, an order of missionaries is itself sent away. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

What happens to an order when the pope himself shuts it down? In a cell in the Castel Sant'Angelo, the old fortress by the Tiber in Rome, sits an elderly priest, Lorenzo Ricci. He is the superior general of the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, the order Ignatius founded, which we met a few weeks back on this path. Except the order he leads no longer exists. The pope has dissolved it. Its houses are closed, its schools taken from it, its priests scattered. Ricci is questioned, kept in custody, and never released. He dies a prisoner. Today, how an order of teachers and missionaries came to this.
screen: `A CELL BY THE TIBER.` → `THE JESUIT GENERAL, A PRISONER.` → `HIS ORDER IS GONE.`

segments.voice: First, the kings. The decisive pressure didn't come from outside the Church. It came from Catholic courts. Portugal, France and Spain had already thrown the Jesuits out of their lands and seized their property. The reasons were tangled: politics, money, quarrels over missions and schools, and resentment of the order's influence. Then those courts pressed the pope to finish the job everywhere. Second, the pen. Pope Clement the Fourteenth gave way. He signed a brief, known by its opening Latin words, Dominus ac Redemptor, the Lord and Redeemer, dissolving the Society for the sake of the peace of the Church. It gave no verdict of heresy. Jesuits in country after country laid down their order's name. They obeyed. Third, the thread that didn't break. In the Russian Empire, Catherine the Great refused to publish the brief, so it never took effect there. A small group of Jesuits carried on there, quietly. Fourth, restored. Decades later, Pope Pius the Seventh restored the Society of Jesus for the whole Church. The same Church that dissolved them brought them back, and the thread from Russia was part of what was rewoven. Saint Paul knew seasons like this. In Second Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but we perish not." Unfair seasons are real. So, in this story, are restorations.
screen: `CATHOLIC KINGS PRESS THE POPE.` · `A BRIEF DISSOLVES THE ORDER.` · `A THREAD SURVIVES IN RUSSIA.` · `RESTORED BY PIUS VII.` · then, large: `CAST DOWN, BUT WE PERISH NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: endure an unfair season. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something unfair you're living with right now. At work, at home, in your body, in a decision someone else made. Name it plainly, without exaggerating and without shrinking it. Then ask what the Jesuits in Russia had to ask: what can I keep doing faithfully, right here, even while it's unfair? One small thing. If you pray, you can place the whole season in God's hands. If you don't, just let yourself hold it without hurrying it. The bell holds the time.
Lorenzo Ricci. The last superior general before the pope dissolved the Jesuits, kept in custody at the Castel Sant'Angelo, who died a prisoner.
Your line: restored. Today, keep doing your one faithful thing inside the unfair season, and remember that the story doesn't end where the brief was signed. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

873.title: The Carmelites of Compiègne (1794)
873.hook: sixteen nuns go to the guillotine singing during the French Revolution
873.howItsDone: Carmelite communities and other Catholics remember the martyrs of Compiègne on their feast day, and performances of Poulenc's Dialogues of the Carmelites keep their story before audiences far beyond the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jesuits suppressed, and their superior Lorenzo Ricci: dissolved under pressure from kings, kept alive in Russia, then restored. Your line was restored. What did you keep doing faithfully in an unfair season? Today, the Revolution comes for a convent. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

Singing, rising over the noise of a Paris crowd. Carts roll toward the guillotine in this season of the Revolution. The crowd is used to shouting, to jeering, to fear. But the women in these carts are singing Latin hymns, the way they sang them in their chapel. Tradition says the crowd grew quiet. These are Carmelite nuns from the town of Compiègne, north of Paris. Their convent was closed. Their habits were taken. They are going to their deaths, and they are singing.
screen: `CARTS TOWARD THE GUILLOTINE.` → `THE WOMEN ARE SINGING.` → `THE CROWD GROWS QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the closed convent. The revolutionary government shut down religious houses, and the Carmelites of Compiègne were turned out. They split into small groups in town, wore ordinary clothes, and kept praying their hours together as best they could, quietly. Second, the offering. Their prioress, Mother Teresa of Saint Augustine, had proposed something before the danger came close: that the community offer themselves to God for peace, for France and for the Church. Tradition says some of the sisters were afraid at first. In the end, they joined. Third, the trial. They were arrested, taken to Paris and brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal. Among the charges was fanaticism. Tradition says one sister asked what the word meant, was told it meant attachment to their religion, and was glad to be condemned for that. Fourth, the scaffold. Tradition says they sang the Veni Creator on the way, and at the foot of the scaffold each sister knelt before the prioress, renewed her vows, and climbed, while those still waiting sang on. The prioress went last. One of the songs tradition gives them is a short psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people." The Church later declared them blessed, and Pope Francis declared them saints. Their story was retold in a play by Georges Bernanos and an opera by Francis Poulenc, Dialogues of the Carmelites. But before any stage, there was a real cart, and real voices, and a hymn that didn't stop.
screen: `A CONVENT CLOSED.` · `AN OFFERING FOR PEACE.` · `CONDEMNED FOR FANATICISM.` · `ONE BY ONE, SINGING.` · then, large: `O PRAISE THE LORD, ALL YE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing in a hard moment. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something hard in front of you: a conversation, a test, a diagnosis, a long day. Then hum, or sing very quietly, one line of a song or hymn you know by heart. Not a performance. Just a voice, held steady. Notice what happens to your breathing while you sing. If you pray, you can sing the psalm's line the Carmelites sang. If you don't, any steady song will do. The bell holds the time.
Laudate Dominum. Praise the Lord, the opening of the psalm tradition says the Carmelites of Compiègne sang on their way to the guillotine.
Your line: singing to the scaffold. Today, when a hard moment comes, keep one line of a song with you, and let it hold your breath steady. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

874.title: Benedict Joseph Labre (1748–1783)
874.hook: rejected by monasteries, he lived as a holy beggar on the streets of Rome
874.howItsDone: Catholics who serve people experiencing homelessness sometimes invoke Saint Benedict Joseph Labre, and his relics and tomb are kept in the church of Santa Maria ai Monti in Rome, near where he died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Carmelites of Compiègne, who sang Laudate Dominum on their way to the guillotine. Your line was singing to the scaffold. Did a song steady you somewhere hard? Today, a saint the crowds walked past. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

Night in Rome, among the broken arches of the Colosseum. In a niche in the stone, a man in rags is asleep. His coat is torn, his hair is matted, a rosary hangs around his neck, and in a small sack he carries a few prayer books and not much else. By day you'll find him in the city's churches, kneeling very still for hours before the Blessed Sacrament. People step around him. Some hold their noses. A few drop a coin, and tradition says he often gives it away to someone poorer. His name is Benedict Joseph Labre.
screen: `ASLEEP IN THE COLOSSEUM.` → `KNEELING FOR HOURS.` → `PEOPLE STEP AROUND HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the doors that closed. Benedict Joseph grew up in northern France and wanted one thing: to be a monk. He knocked at Carthusian houses and at Trappist monasteries. He was turned away, or he was taken in and then fell ill and had to leave. Again and again, the door he was sure God wanted kept closing. Second, the road. So he stopped knocking and started walking. He became a pilgrim, going on foot from shrine to shrine across Europe, sleeping outdoors, begging only what he needed for the day. He said little. He prayed constantly. Third, Rome. In the end he stayed in Rome, sleeping in the ruins and spending his days in its churches. He looked like what he was: a homeless man. Some called him a madman or a fraud. Jesus said of himself, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests: but the son of man hath not where to lay his head." Labre took that line and lived inside it. Fourth, the saint is dead. During Holy Week he collapsed near a church and was carried into a nearby house, where he died. Tradition says children ran through the streets crying, the saint is dead. People who had stepped around him came to his funeral. The Church later declared him a saint. Some Catholics read him alongside Matthew twenty-five, where Jesus says: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." In that reading, Labre was the stranger.
screen: `THE MONASTERY DOORS CLOSE.` · `A PILGRIM ON FOOT.` · `A HOMELESS MAN IN ROME.` · `THE SAINT IS DEAD.` · then, large: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a homeless person. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone without a home you've passed recently, at a station, outside a shop, on a bench. Try to remember their face, not just their sign or their bags. Maybe you don't know their name. That's all right. Hold them in your mind as a person with a story you haven't heard. Then decide one small thing for the next time: eye contact, a greeting, asking their name. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Pilgrim. What Benedict Joseph Labre became after monasteries turned him away: a beggar walking from shrine to shrine, sleeping outdoors, praying constantly.
Your line: the holy beggar. Today, when you pass someone asking for help, slow down long enough to see a face, whether or not you give anything. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

875.title: The Korean church (1784)
875.hook: founded by laypeople who read Catholic books before any priest arrived
875.howItsDone: Korean Catholics honor their martyrs, lay and ordained, with shrines and pilgrimages, and the Church keeps a feast of Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang and companions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict Joseph Labre, the pilgrim who slept in the Colosseum and prayed in Rome's churches. Your line was the holy beggar. Did you slow down long enough to see a face? Today, a church that began with a stack of books. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

Korean envoys come home from Beijing with books in their baggage. They're written in Chinese, the language of learning in Korea. Some are about the stars, some about mathematics. And some are about a faith that calls God the Lord of Heaven, written by missionaries in China, among them Matteo Ricci, the Jesuit in a scholar's robe from earlier on this path. In Korea, a circle of scholars starts reading them, arguing about them, and slowly, praying with them. There isn't a single priest in the country. Nobody has come to preach. They have only the books.
screen: `BOOKS FROM BEIJING.` → `THE LORD OF HEAVEN.` → `NO PRIEST IN THE COUNTRY.`

segments.voice: First, faith by reading. These Korean scholars weren't converted by a missionary. They studied their way in, meeting to read, question and discuss. Saint Paul wrote, in the Douay-Rheims: "Faith then cometh by hearing; and hearing by the word of Christ." Here, the hearing came through pages. Second, a baptism in Beijing. They knew a Christian needs baptism, and they had no one to give it. So one of them, Yi Seung-hun, traveled with a diplomatic mission to Beijing, asked for baptism there, and received the name Peter. He came home and baptized his friends. Third, a church with no clergy. Laypeople taught, gathered, and led. Tradition says they even began appointing priests among themselves and celebrating sacraments, until they learned that only an ordained priest could. They stopped, wrote to the bishop of Beijing, and asked him to send one. When a priest finally came in secret, he found a church already waiting. Fourth, a church of martyrs. The Korean government saw the new faith as a threat to the social order and to honoring ancestors, and waves of persecution followed. Laypeople and priests died for it, among them Andrew Kim Taegon, a Korean priest, and Paul Chong Hasang, a layman who worked to bring priests into the country. The Church later declared them saints together. In Korea, the faith wasn't carried in by clergy and handed down. Ordinary readers went looking for it, and then sent for a priest.
screen: `FAITH BY READING.` · `A BAPTISM IN BEIJING.` · `A CHURCH RUN BY LAYPEOPLE.` · `A CHURCH OF MARTYRS.` · then, large: `FAITH THEN COMETH BY HEARING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a spiritual book, slowly. Settle, and breathe. Pick up whatever is close: a Gospel, a book of a saint's life, a book of prayers, a page saved on your phone. If you have nothing nearby, open the Gospel of Mark to its first page. Read a few lines, then stop. Read them again. Let one sentence stand out, the way a line caught those scholars. Don't try to finish anything. If you pray, you can turn that sentence into a quiet conversation with God. The bell holds the time.
Yi Seung-hun. The Korean scholar who traveled to Beijing, asked for baptism, took the name Peter, and came home to baptize his friends.

Your line: laypeople first. This week went from Alphonsus's mercy and Montfort's road, through Serra told honestly, the Jesuits restored, the Carmelites singing and a holy beggar, to readers in Korea. Today, read one more page of your book, on your own. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

fork.setup: you're one of the Korean scholars. you've read the books and want baptism, and there's no priest anywhere in the country. what do you do?
options: wait, and hope a priest comes someday.
send one of you to Beijing to be baptized, and bring it home.
give up, since there's no one to baptize you.
fork.reveal: Yi Seung-hun went with a diplomatic mission to Beijing, was baptized there as Peter, and came home to baptize his friends.

original.note: Korean: the teaching of the Lord of Heaven, the Korean name for the Catholic faith.

trapdoor: what you thought: missionaries brought the faith to Korea.
what it means: Korean laypeople found it in books, baptized one another, and then sent for a priest.
what a scholar hears: Chinese Catholic books, a baptism in Beijing, a lay-led church that asked Beijing for clergy, and a long season of martyrdom.
